home.sub: Research, travel, company set-up, customs, approvals, sales and scale — one operator for the whole journey into Pakistan, India, the Philippines and the UAE.
premise: A manufacturer in Dongguan can find an agent in an office in Karachi tomorrow. What is hard to find is someone who will be standing in the shop when the first container lands, and again when the third one does.

We are three people who met in Guangzhou and then spent fifteen years apart — building electronics, solar and retail businesses in Pakistan, India, the Philippines, and now the UAE. We know what a phone shop in Saddar will actually stock, and why a battery that sells in Manila fails in Bihar.
TGO owns and builds the brands, handles certification and channel, and carries the warranty. The parent stays invisible. The brands do the talking.

what.title: The bridge.
what.sub: Five things, described plainly. If one of them is what you need, the next section tells you exactly how it starts.

pillars.w: For manufacturers and brand owners with a product that already sells somewhere.
pillars.d: We put Chinese products into shops in Pakistan, India, the Philippines, and now the UAE — the real channel, not a warehouse. Modern trade where it exists, and the ten-thousand-shop informal trade where it does not, which in our markets is most of it.

pillars.w: For factories that make well and market badly.
pillars.d: We build and own brands under TGO: naming, packaging, price architecture, warranty terms, retail training. You keep making the product. The brand belongs to the market it sells in.

pillars.w: For anyone who has been told "just find a distributor".
pillars.d: Certification (BIS in India, PSQCA in Pakistan, BPS in the Philippines, plus UAE market entry), duty and landed-cost modelling, channel strategy, warranty and after-sales structure. This is the work that decides whether the first shipment becomes the tenth.

pillars.w: For retailers and brands who need a factory, not a market.
pillars.d: We qualify and manage Chinese manufacturers on your behalf: factory audits, price negotiation, QC on the line, and consolidated shipping. You get a vetted supply chain without the years it takes to build one yourself.

pillars.w: For teams who need to see a market before they commit to it.
pillars.d: We take your team on the ground in Pakistan, India, the Philippines or the UAE to survey the real conditions — retail, competition, pricing — then help set up the local company needed to expand there.

what.startNote: Almost nobody publishes this. Manufacturers ask us for it in the first meeting, so here it is.

steps.d: Thirty minutes on video or in your factory. Category, capacity, what you have already tried, what went wrong. No documents.
We take samples into the market and put them in front of real buyers in 2–3 weeks. You get their answers unedited, including the ones you will not like.
One container or less, priced properly, sold through our channel. We learn the true landed cost, the sell-through rate and the return rate before anyone commits.
Volume bands, exclusivity where it is earned, warranty terms, marketing split. Written in plain language, one market at a time.

what.proofKicker: What this looks like in practice
proof: A Shenzhen lithium-battery manufacturer with 400 staff, exporting to 14 countries, needed a route into Pakistan. They had two failed distributor relationships and no local certification.
A Guangzhou accessories factory producing for three European private labels wanted its own brand in South Asia rather than another OEM contract.

founders.title: We met in China.
founders.sub: Two brothers and a lifelong friend, 2006 onward. This is the part of the company that is not a structure.

acts.d: Guangzhou, 2006. Trade fairs, sample rooms, and the long bus ride out to Dongguan. We learned the business the way it is actually learned — badly at first, in canteens, from people who had no reason to help us and did anyway.

Umair went home to Pakistan and built electronics, solar and lithium ventures. Umer went to Manila and stayed 10+ years, building distribution and a travel business. Aryan went to India, spent years at Oppo in Bihar, then founded his own technology company.
2026. Three markets between us, three sets of mistakes already paid for, and one shared view: the gap is not products and it is not factories. It is trust that survives the second shipment.

people.bio: Fronts the TGO channel and runs the Pakistan market. Built and operates Bulk Gurus and Group ventures across electronics, solar and lithium storage. Handles manufacturer relationships in China and anything to do with putting a brand on a shelf for the first time.

markets.title: Four markets we live in.
markets.sub: Not a list of opportunities. What is actually true about selling here, including the parts that are hard.

items.size: ~240M people · median age ~20 · consumer electronics import market $2.4B
items.retail: Overwhelmingly general trade. Mobile retail clusters — Saddar in Karachi, Hafeez Centre in Lahore — set the price the whole country pays. Modern trade is under 10% of the category.
items.hard: Import duty structure changes with the budget. Dollar availability and LC delays can strand a shipment for weeks. Warranty culture is thin, which means a brand that honours warranty is remembered for it.
items.have: Existing distribution relationships across 4 cities, PSQCA experience, and a founder who has been importing into this market for over a decade.

items.size: ~1.43B people · the world’s second-largest smartphone market · accessories market growing ~14% CAGR
items.retail: Distributor–dealer hierarchies that are precise and unforgiving about margin. Regional strength matters more than national presence: winning Bihar and UP is a different business from winning Bangalore.
items.hard: BIS registration is mandatory and slow — plan on 8–16 weeks before it is a market at all. GST and state-level logistics add real complexity. Price sensitivity at the entry tier is brutal.
items.have: Ex-Oppo channel knowledge in Bihar, an operating company on the ground, and BIS filings in progress for the solar line.

items.size: ~115M people · 7,600 islands · among the world’s highest social-commerce adoption
items.retail: More concentrated than South Asia: national chains and mall retail matter, alongside sari-sari stores at the smallest end. Live-selling and marketplace commerce are not a channel experiment here, they are the channel.
items.hard: Island logistics turn one country into three distribution problems. BPS certification and import documentation are strict. Typhoon season is a real line in the plan.
items.have: Ten-plus years of resident operations in Manila, warehousing and last-mile relationships, and a founder who lives there.

items.size: ~10M people · high-income, high e-commerce penetration · gateway to the wider GCC
items.retail: Amazon.ae and Noon dominate online; Dubai and Sharjah malls anchor offline. A demanding, brand-aware buyer used to fast delivery and easy returns.
items.hard: Marketplace competition is fierce and margin-thin. Amazon/Noon account health, ad spend and review velocity all need constant management.
items.have: A guest team member resident in the UAE since 2008, running Amazon and Noon accounts and consulting on online brand growth and sales scaling.

insights.title: Notes from the route.
insights.sub: Weekly, tied to the channel. Written from the road, not from a keyword list.

posts.t: What a phone shop in Saddar will actually stock
posts.ex: Six SKUs, and none of them are the one your marketing deck is built around. A morning spent counting what is on the counter.

posts.t: The sample that passes and the container that fails
posts.ex: How golden samples drift, why it is usually not dishonesty, and the two checks that catch it before the shipment.

posts.t: Why the parent company stays invisible
posts.ex: BBK sells more phones than almost anyone and nobody asks for a BBK. Why we structured TGO the same way.

posts.t: BIS is not a formality, it is a calendar
posts.ex: What the India certification clock actually looks like, and how to run it in parallel instead of in sequence.
